title: "Smooth Morphisms Again"
subtitle: ""

## Notation and local models

No global Noetherian hypothesis is needed below; the relevant finiteness
assumptions are stated explicitly. For a morphism $\pi:X\to Y$, write

$$
\Omega_{X/Y}=\Omega^1_{X/Y}
$$

for the sheaf of relative Kähler differentials. If $y\in Y$, then

$$
X_y := X\times_Y \operatorname{Spec}\kappa(y)
$$

denotes the fiber over $y$. A *geometric fiber* is the further base change
$X_{\bar y}=X_y\times_{\kappa(y)}\overline{\kappa(y)}$.

::: {#def-standard-smooth}

Let $R$ be a ring and let

$$
B=
\frac{R[x_1,\ldots,x_{n+r}]}{(f_1,\ldots,f_r)}.
$$

The morphism

$$
\operatorname{Spec}B\longrightarrow \operatorname{Spec}R
$$

is **standard smooth of relative dimension $n$** if some $r\times r$
minor of the Jacobian matrix

$$
J(f)=
\left(\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_j}\right)_
{\substack{1\le i\le r\\1\le j\le n+r}}
$$

is invertible in $B$. After reordering the variables, one may assume that

$$
\det\left(\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_j}\right)_{1\le i,j\le r}
\in B^\times.
$$

A morphism is smooth of relative dimension $n$ precisely when it is locally,
on both source and target, of this form.
:::

For a standard smooth presentation, the conormal sequence is

$$
(f_1,\ldots,f_r)/(f_1,\ldots,f_r)^2
\longrightarrow
\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n+r}B\,dx_j
\longrightarrow
\Omega_{B/R}
\longrightarrow 0.
$$

The invertible Jacobian minor allows $dx_1,\ldots,dx_r$ to be eliminated.
Consequently,

$$
\Omega_{B/R}\cong
\bigoplus_{j=r+1}^{n+r}B\,dx_j,
$$

so $\Omega_{B/R}$ is locally free of rank $n$.

## A zero-dimensional smooth immersion

::: {#lem-smooth-immersion}
### Smooth locally closed immersions

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a locally closed immersion. Then $f$ is smooth of
relative dimension $0$ if and only if $f$ is an open immersion.
:::

::: {.proof}
Every open immersion is smooth of relative dimension $0$, so only the
converse needs proof.

There is a short conceptual argument. A locally closed immersion is a
monomorphism. A smooth morphism of relative dimension $0$ is étale, and an
étale monomorphism is an open immersion.

The following affine calculation records the Jacobian argument behind this
fact. Because the assertion is local on $X$ and $Y$, shrink around a point
of $X$ so that $f$ is both a closed immersion and standard smooth of
relative dimension $0$. We may write

$$
X=\operatorname{Spec}B,
\qquad
Y=\operatorname{Spec}R,
\qquad
B=\frac{R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]}{(f_1,\ldots,f_n)},
$$

with

$$
\det J(f)=
\det\left(\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_j}\right)_{1\le i,j\le n}
\in B^\times.
$$

Since $X\to Y$ is a closed immersion, the ring map $R\to B$ is
surjective. Hence, for every $i$, there exists $r_i\in R$ and
$a_{ij}\in R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ such that

$$
x_i=r_i+\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}f_j.
$$

Differentiate with respect to $x_\ell$:

$$
\delta_{i\ell}
=
\sum_{j=1}^n
\left(
\frac{\partial a_{ij}}{\partial x_\ell}f_j
+a_{ij}\frac{\partial f_j}{\partial x_\ell}
\right).
$$

Modulo $(f_1,\ldots,f_n)$, this becomes the matrix identity

$$
I_n=
(a_{ij})_{i,j}
\left(\frac{\partial f_j}{\partial x_\ell}\right)_{j,\ell}
\qquad\text{in }M_n(B).
$$

The Jacobian matrix is invertible in $B$, so $(a_{ij})$ is invertible in
$B$ as well. After possibly shrinking once more, the two ideals agree:

$$
(f_1,\ldots,f_n)
=
(x_1-r_1,\ldots,x_n-r_n).
$$

Therefore

$$
B
\cong
\frac{R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]}
{(x_1-r_1,\ldots,x_n-r_n)}
\cong R.
$$

Thus $f$ is locally an isomorphism onto an open subscheme of $Y$. Hence
$f$ is an open immersion.
:::

::: {#rem-etale-language}
## Étale interpretation

The lemma is often summarized as

$$
\text{étale monomorphism}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{open immersion}.
$$

The relative-dimension-zero hypothesis is exactly what turns a smooth
morphism into an étale morphism.
:::

## Equivalent criteria for smoothness

::: {#thm-smooth-criteria}
### Fiberwise and differential criteria

Let $\pi:X\to Y$ be a morphism of schemes, and let $n\ge 0$. The following
conditions are equivalent.

1. $\pi$ is smooth of relative dimension $n$.

2. $\pi$ is locally of finite presentation and flat, its fibers have pure
   dimension $n$, and $\Omega_{X/Y}$ is locally free of rank $n$.

3. $\pi$ is locally of finite presentation and flat, and every fiber $X_y$
   is a smooth $\kappa(y)$-scheme of pure dimension $n$.

4. $\pi$ is locally of finite presentation and flat, and every geometric
   fiber $X_{\bar y}$ is a smooth $\overline{\kappa(y)}$-scheme of pure
   dimension $n$.
:::

::: {.proof}
We follow the chain

$$
(1)\Longrightarrow(2)\Longrightarrow(3)
\Longleftrightarrow(4),
\qquad
(3)\Longrightarrow(1).
$$

#### Step 1: $(1)\Rightarrow(2)$

Smooth morphisms are locally of finite presentation and flat. Locally, $\pi$
has a standard smooth presentation

$$
B=
\frac{R[x_1,\ldots,x_{n+r}]}{(f_1,\ldots,f_r)}.
$$

By the Jacobian calculation following @def-standard-smooth,
$\Omega_{B/R}$ is free of rank $n$. Standard smooth morphisms have fibers
of pure dimension $n$, so condition (2) follows.

#### Step 2: $(2)\Rightarrow(3)$

Fix $y\in Y$. Formation of Kähler differentials commutes with base change:

$$
\Omega_{X_y/\kappa(y)}
\cong
\Omega_{X/Y}|_{X_y}.
$$

Thus $\Omega_{X_y/\kappa(y)}$ is locally free of rank $n$. Since $X_y$
is of finite type and pure dimension $n$, the differential form of the
Jacobian criterion shows that $X_y$ is smooth over $\kappa(y)$.

#### Step 3: $(3)\Longleftrightarrow(4)$

Smoothness and pure relative dimension are preserved by arbitrary base change,
so (3) implies (4). Conversely, smoothness descends along the faithfully flat
field extension

$$
\kappa(y)\subseteq \overline{\kappa(y)}.
$$

Dimension is unchanged under algebraic field extension. Therefore (4) implies
(3).

#### Step 4: $(3)\Rightarrow(1)$

Fix $p\in X$, and put $q=\pi(p)$. Because $\pi$ is locally of finite
presentation, after shrinking around $p$ and $q$ we can write

$$
U=\operatorname{Spec}C
\longrightarrow
V=\operatorname{Spec}B,
\qquad
C=\frac{B[x_1,\ldots,x_N]}{I},
$$

where $I=(f_1,\ldots,f_s)$ is finitely generated. Passing to the fiber over
$q$ gives

$$
\overline U
=
U\times_V\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(q)
=
\operatorname{Spec}
\frac{\kappa(q)[x_1,\ldots,x_N]}{\overline I}.
$$

By (3), $\overline U$ is smooth of dimension $n$ at $p$. The Jacobian
criterion therefore supplies

$$
r=N-n
$$

elements of $\overline I$, which we may take to be
$\overline f_1,\ldots,\overline f_r$, such that an $r\times r$ Jacobian
minor is invertible near $p$. Lift these elements to
$f_1,\ldots,f_r\in I$, and localize so that the same minor is invertible.
Set

$$
R=
\frac{B[x_1,\ldots,x_N]}{(f_1,\ldots,f_r)},
\qquad
J=I/(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\subseteq R.
$$

Then $\operatorname{Spec}R\to\operatorname{Spec}B$ is standard smooth of
relative dimension $n$, while

$$
C\cong R/J.
$$

On the fiber over $q$, the two schemes agree in a neighborhood of $p$, so

$$
(J\otimes_B\kappa(q))_p=0.
$$

Here is where flatness is essential. From

$$
0\longrightarrow J\longrightarrow R\longrightarrow C\longrightarrow 0
$$

and the flatness of $C$ over $B$, tensoring with $\kappa(q)$ remains
exact on the left. Hence the displayed vanishing is genuine, rather than being
obscured by a $\operatorname{Tor}_1^B(C,\kappa(q))$ term. Equivalently,

$$
J_p=\mathfrak m_qJ_p.
$$

Since $J_p$ is a finite module over the local ring $R_p$, Nakayama's lemma
gives $J_p=0$. After shrinking around $p$, we have $J=0$, and hence

$$
U\cong\operatorname{Spec}R
$$

is standard smooth of relative dimension $n$ over $V$. As $p$ was
arbitrary, $\pi$ is smooth of relative dimension $n$.
:::

::: {#rem-closed-points}
In a fiber of finite type over a field, closed points are dense. Thus one may
also run Step 4 first at closed points of the fibers. The standard smooth locus
is open, and a nonempty closed subset of a finite-type fiber contains a closed
point; consequently, covering all closed points covers the whole fiber.
:::

## Formal smoothness

::: {#def-formally-smooth}
A morphism $\pi:X\to Y$ is **formally smooth** if the following lifting
property holds. For every affine $Y$-scheme $T$ and every closed subscheme
$T_0\hookrightarrow T$ defined by a quasi-coherent ideal sheaf
$\mathcal J$ with $\mathcal J^2=0$, the restriction map

$$
\operatorname{Hom}_Y(T,X)
\longrightarrow
\operatorname{Hom}_Y(T_0,X)
$$

is surjective.

Equivalently, every commutative diagram

$$
\begin{array}{ccc}
T_0 & \longrightarrow & X\\
\big\downarrow & & \big\downarrow\!\pi\\
T & \longrightarrow & Y
\end{array}
$$

admits a dotted lift $T\to X$.
:::

On affine schemes, with $Y=\operatorname{Spec}R$ and
$X=\operatorname{Spec}B$, formal smoothness says: for every $R$-algebra
$C$, every square-zero ideal $J\subseteq C$, and every $R$-algebra map

$$
B\longrightarrow C/J,
$$

there exists an $R$-algebra lift $B\to C$.

::: {#thm-smooth-formally-smooth}
A morphism $\pi:X\to Y$ is smooth if and only if it is locally of finite
presentation and formally smooth.
:::

::: {.proof}
We first verify the lifting property for a standard smooth affine morphism.
Let

$$
A=R[x_1,\ldots,x_{n+r}],
\qquad
I=(f_1,\ldots,f_r),
\qquad
B=A/I,
$$

where an $r\times r$ Jacobian minor is invertible in $B$. Let $C$ be an
$R$-algebra, let $J\subseteq C$ satisfy $J^2=0$, and suppose that we are
given

$$
\varphi:B\longrightarrow C/J.
$$

Because $A$ is a polynomial algebra, choose arbitrary lifts in $C$ of the
images of the variables. They define an $R$-algebra map

$$
\psi:A\longrightarrow C
$$

lifting $A\to B\xrightarrow{\varphi}C/J$. Since $\psi(I)\subseteq J$ and
$J^2=0$, the restriction of $\psi$ induces a $B$-linear map

$$
\overline\psi:I/I^2\longrightarrow J.
$$

For a standard smooth algebra, the conormal sequence

$$
0\longrightarrow I/I^2
\longrightarrow \Omega_{A/R}\otimes_A B
\longrightarrow \Omega_{B/R}
\longrightarrow 0
$$

is split exact. Hence $\overline\psi$ extends to a $B$-linear map

$$
\Omega_{A/R}\otimes_A B\longrightarrow J.
$$

By the universal property of Kähler differentials, this extension corresponds
to an $R$-derivation

$$
\delta:A\longrightarrow J
$$

whose restriction to $I$ equals $\psi|_I$. Therefore

$$
\psi-\delta:A\longrightarrow C
$$

vanishes on $I$, so it factors through $B=A/I$. The resulting map
$B\to C$ is the desired lift of $\varphi$. Thus every standard smooth
morphism is formally smooth, and therefore every smooth morphism is formally
smooth.

Conversely, suppose that $B$ is a finitely presented, formally smooth
$R$-algebra. Choose a finite presentation

$$
B=A/I,
\qquad
A=R[x_1,\ldots,x_N].
$$

Apply formal smoothness to the square-zero extension

$$
A/I^2\longrightarrow A/I=B,
\qquad
\ker(A/I^2\to A/I)=I/I^2.
$$

The identity map of $B$ lifts to an $R$-algebra section

$$
B\longrightarrow A/I^2.
$$

This infinitesimal section yields a splitting of the conormal sequence

$$
0\longrightarrow I/I^2
\longrightarrow \Omega_{A/R}\otimes_A B
\longrightarrow \Omega_{B/R}
\longrightarrow 0.
$$

Because the middle term is finite free, $\Omega_{B/R}$ is finite projective.
More concretely, fix $p\in\operatorname{Spec}B$. After localizing, choose
$f_1,\ldots,f_r\in I$ whose classes form a basis of $I/I^2$. Nakayama's
lemma shows that these elements generate $I$ near $p$. Since the inclusion

$$
I/I^2\longrightarrow\Omega_{A/R}\otimes_A B
$$

is a split injection, its Jacobian matrix has rank $r$; after shrinking, some
$r\times r$ minor is invertible. Thus $B$ has a standard smooth
presentation near $p$. It follows that $B$ is smooth over $R$, and the
scheme-theoretic statement follows by working affine-locally.
:::

::: {#rem-finiteness-essential}
Formal smoothness alone is not equivalent to smoothness. For example,

$$
R[x_1,x_2,x_3,\ldots]
$$

is formally smooth over $R$, but it is not finitely presented over $R$, so
its spectrum is not smooth over $\operatorname{Spec}R$ in the usual
scheme-theoretic sense. Thus the precise statement is

$$
\boxed{
\text{smooth}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{locally of finite presentation + formally smooth}
}.
$$
:::

## Injection of the morphism between fibres of the sheaves of differntials


## Logical map of the note

The main implications can be kept in view as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{standard smooth}
&\Longrightarrow
\Omega_{X/Y}\text{ locally free of the expected rank},\\
\text{flat + smooth fibers}
&\Longrightarrow
\text{standard smooth locally},\\
\text{standard smooth}
&\Longrightarrow
\text{square-zero lifting},\\
\text{finite presentation + square-zero lifting}
&\Longrightarrow
\text{smooth}.
\end{aligned}
$$

In relative dimension $0$, smoothness becomes étaleness; imposing the
monomorphism condition supplied by an immersion then forces the morphism to be
an open immersion, as in @lem-smooth-immersion.
